title: API design and security
blurb: The OWASP API Top 10, rate limiting, idempotency and webhook security, built rather than recited.

questions.q: In code review you see this Express handler behind a working login middleware. Which change closes its authorization hole?
choices: Switch invoice ids to random UUIDs so that nobody can guess another invoice
Validate that `req.params.id` is a positive integer before querying the table
Look the invoice up by id and the caller's account id, returning 404 if absent
Rate-limit the route so a user cannot walk through thousands of ids per minute
questions.why: Any logged-in user can read any invoice by changing the id: the handler checks who you are, never whether the record is yours. Scope the query to the owner (or check ownership after loading) on every object access. UUIDs and rate limits only slow enumeration; a leaked or shared id still opens the record.
questions.asked: The top API risk as a code-review exercise; strong candidates also say where the ownership check should live so it is not forgotten per route.

questions.q: This profile-update endpoint lets users edit their name and bio. What can an attacker do with it?
choices: Send `"role": "admin"` or `"emailVerified": true` and have it saved as well
Update another user's profile by putting a different id in the request body
Nothing serious, since the update is already scoped to the caller's own row
Crash the server by sending a JSON body that nests objects very deeply
questions.why: Passing `req.body` straight to the update is mass assignment (over-posting): every column the ORM knows about is writable, including ones the form never shows. Map the body onto an allow-listed DTO of editable fields. The row is scoped to the caller, so the attack is privilege escalation on their own account, not editing someone else's.
questions.asked: Mass assignment is a common real finding; interviewers want to hear 'DTO allow-list', not 'strip the role field'.

questions.q: `GET /users/42` returns the full user row, including `passwordHash` and `resetToken`, and the React app only displays the name. What is the flaw?
choices: The API exposes properties the caller may not see; the server must shape it
The response should be gzipped so the sensitive fields are harder to read
None in practice, because the UI never renders the hash or the reset token
The fields should be base64-encoded so they are not readable in DevTools
questions.why: Anything in the response is readable in DevTools or with curl, whatever the UI renders. OWASP groups this with mass assignment as broken object property level authorization: the server decides which properties each caller may read or write, usually with a response DTO. Compression and base64 are encodings, not access control.
questions.asked: Checks that you treat the client as untrusted in both directions, not only for input.

questions.q: The UI shows the 'Delete user' button only to admins, but `DELETE /api/users/:id` checks only that the caller is logged in. Which OWASP API risk is this?
choices: Broken object-level authorization, since the target user record is not checked
Security misconfiguration, since the route should have been disabled in production
Broken function-level authorization: a privileged operation lacks a role check
Broken authentication, since the login middleware should have rejected the call
questions.why: Function-level authorization asks whether this caller may perform this operation at all, and hiding a button is not a control, because anyone can send the request. BOLA is about which record; here no user record would be safe from a non-admin. Put role or permission checks on the route or in a policy, and deny admin routes by default.
questions.asked: Separates BOLA from BFLA, which many candidates blur; a strong answer mentions deny-by-default admin routes.

questions.q: A list endpoint passes `limit` from the query string straight to the database. What is the main risk, and the usual fix?
questions.code:
const limit = Number(req.query.limit ?? 20);
const rows = await db.orders.findMany({ take: limit, skip: offset });
choices: SQL injection through `limit`; fix it by escaping the value before the query
`?limit=5000000` exhausts memory and the DB; clamp it to a maximum such as 100
Clients can skip pages; fix it by making `limit` a fixed value on the server
Negative values reveal deleted rows; fix it by rejecting any `limit` below 1
questions.why: OWASP calls this unrestricted resource consumption: one request can load millions of rows, hold a connection and spike memory. Clamp page size (and validate it is a positive integer) server-side, and cap body size, upload size and query cost the same way. `Number()` plus an ORM parameter is not an injection vector here.
questions.asked: A cheap, very common gap; interviewers like hearing that every client-controlled size has a server-side ceiling.

questions.q: Customers can register a webhook URL that your backend POSTs to on events. Which attack does that feature open up?
choices: Cross-site scripting, since the URL is later rendered in the customer's dashboard
Clickjacking, since the target page can be framed inside your settings screen
Cross-site request forgery, since the POST carries your server's session cookies
Server-side request forgery: your server can be aimed at internal-only addresses
questions.why: Any feature where the server fetches a URL the user supplied lets the user choose what your server talks to: `http://169.254.169.254/` (cloud metadata), an admin service on the private network, or localhost. Validate the resolved address against private ranges, disable redirects or re-check them, and ideally send through an egress proxy. CSRF needs a victim's browser, not your server.
questions.asked: SSRF hides in features like webhooks, imports and link previews; interviewers look for spotting it in a product feature, not only by name.

questions.q: Your API enriches orders with data from a partner's shipping API. What does OWASP's 'unsafe consumption of APIs' warn you to do?
choices: Validate its responses, set timeouts, and avoid blindly following its redirects
Trust its responses fully, since the partner is contractually vetted and signed
Call it only from the browser, so that its failures never touch your own server
Cache every response forever, so that a compromise of the partner cannot reach you
questions.why: Developers often validate user input but trust third-party responses, so a compromised or buggy partner becomes an injection or SSRF path into your system. Treat its data as untrusted input (schema-validate, encode on output), use TLS, bound timeouts and response sizes, and do not follow redirects blindly. A contract does not stop a breach on their side.
questions.asked: Shows whether trust boundaries in your head include your own dependencies, not just the public internet.

questions.q: A partner's nightly batch job must call your API with no user present. Why pick OAuth client credentials over a static API key?
choices: Client credentials let the partner log in as each of your end users in turn
Its tokens are short-lived and scoped, so a leaked token expires on its own
API keys cannot be sent over HTTPS, while bearer tokens are always encrypted
Client credentials need no secret at all, so there is nothing that can leak
questions.why: The partner swaps its client secret for an access token that expires in minutes and carries only the scopes granted, and your API validates it like any other token. A static key is valid until someone rotates it by hand. The client secret still exists, and there is no user: this flow is machine-to-machine only.
questions.asked: Machine-to-machine auth comes up for any integration role; a strong answer still says API keys are fine for simple, low-risk cases.

questions.q: You store API keys as SHA-256 hashes and show each key once at creation. Why is a fast hash acceptable here, when it is wrong for passwords?
choices: SHA-256 is only unsafe for short inputs, and API keys are always long strings
API keys are never stolen from databases, because they are rarely used by people
A slow hash would break the constant-time comparison that the API relies on
Keys are long random strings, so there is no guessable space to brute-force
questions.why: Slow hashes exist to make guessing human-chosen passwords expensive. A 32-byte random key has 256 bits of entropy, so even billions of SHA-256 guesses per second get nowhere, and a fast hash keeps per-request lookup cheap. Add a visible prefix (such as `sk_live_`) so leaked keys are easy to scan for.
questions.asked: Tests whether you know why password hashing is slow, rather than applying bcrypt to every secret by rule.

questions.q: An access token carries the scope `invoices:read`. What does the scope tell your API?
choices: Which invoices this user owns, so the API can skip its own ownership check
Which operations the client was granted; object ownership is checked separately
Which database tables the token is allowed to query directly without the API
Which API version the client was built against, for routing to older handlers
questions.why: A scope limits what a client (and the user who consented) may do: read invoices, not write them. It says nothing about which invoice, so a token with `invoices:read` must still be refused someone else's invoice. Check scope per route, then ownership per object.
questions.asked: Candidates often treat scopes as full authorization; the follow-up is usually 'so where does BOLA get checked?'

questions.q: Your API receives a bearer JWT from your identity provider. Which checks are the minimum before trusting its claims?
choices: Signature only, since a valid signature proves every claim inside is acceptable
That it decodes to JSON containing `sub` and `iat`, then load the user by `sub`
`exp` and `sub` alone, since the payload cannot be edited without breaking it
Signature with a pinned algorithm, then `iss`, `aud` and `exp` with a small skew
questions.why: The signature proves who minted the token, not that it was minted for you or is still valid: check the issuer, that the audience is this API, and expiry (allowing a minute or so of clock skew), with algorithms pinned. Decoding without verifying accepts forged tokens, and signature-only accepts tokens issued for another API by the same provider.
questions.asked: The JWT validation checklist is a standard backend screen; listing the claims beats saying 'the library handles it'.

questions.q: Your identity provider rotates its signing keys every 90 days and publishes them at a JWKS URL. How does your API keep verifying tokens across a rotation without a redeploy?
choices: Fetch the JWKS once at startup, since a key rotation invalidates every token issued before it anyway
Cache the JWKS, pick the key by the token's `kid` header, and refetch when an unknown `kid` arrives
Trust the `x5c` certificate in the token's own header, since it carries the public key that signed it
Fall back to the token's `alg` value when no key matches, so verification cannot fail during a rotation
questions.why: `kid` is a label, not a secret: it names which of the provider's published keys signed this token. A cached JWKS with a refetch on unknown `kid` (rate-limited, so attackers cannot force fetches with random ids) verifies old tokens with the old key and new ones with the new key during the overlap. Trusting a key the token carries lets an attacker ship their own; the token's `alg` is never consulted.
questions.asked: Key rotation is where JWT setups break in production; a strong answer names the `kid` lookup, the bounded refetch and why the header can never be the source of the key.

questions.q: A fixed-window limiter allows 100 requests per calendar minute. What can a client do that a sliding window or token bucket would stop?
choices: Send 200 requests in about two seconds, straddling the minute boundary
Avoid the limit completely by opening a new TCP connection per request
Get 100 requests per second, since the window resets on every new second
Consume the quota of other clients, since fixed windows share one counter
questions.why: The counter resets at :00, so 100 requests at 12:00:59 and 100 more at 12:01:00 all pass. A sliding window counts the last 60 seconds from now; a token bucket refills gradually, allowing bursts only up to its capacity. Fixed windows are still fine when a short double burst is harmless, because they are the cheapest to run.
questions.asked: A design question with a concrete flaw to find; follow-ups ask which algorithm you would pick for a login or search endpoint.

questions.q: Your B2B API is used by companies whose staff share one office IP. What should the rate-limit key be for authenticated calls?
choices: The client IP address, since it cannot be changed without real effort
One global counter, so that a single limit protects the whole service
The `User-Agent` header, since it identifies which client app is calling
The API key or user id, keeping IP limits for unauthenticated routes
questions.why: Per-IP limits punish everyone behind one NAT or proxy while one attacker with many IPs walks past them. Once a caller is authenticated, limit on their identity (and possibly per tenant); keep per-IP limits for login, signup and other anonymous routes. `User-Agent` is set by the client, and a global counter lets one tenant starve the rest.
questions.asked: Tests whether you think about who the limit hurts, not just the algorithm.

questions.q: Four API instances each run an in-memory limiter set to 100 requests per minute per user. What limit does a user actually get?
choices: Exactly 100, because the load balancer routes each user to one instance
Exactly 25, because the limit is divided between the four instances
Up to about 400, since each instance counts only what it saw itself
Zero after the first minute, since the four counters conflict and lock
questions.why: Each process keeps its own counter, so round-robin spreads a user's calls across four independent limits. Use a shared store such as Redis, incrementing and setting expiry atomically (INCR plus EXPIRE in one script, or a library that does it), or enforce limits at the gateway. Sticky sessions are not a reliable way to route every request of a user.
questions.asked: A scaling bug that appears only after you add instances; the fix and its atomicity show real experience.

questions.q: A POST with `Idempotency-Key: 7f3a…` succeeded, but the client timed out and resends it with the same key and body. What should the server do?
choices: Return the stored response of the first attempt without running the logic again
Process the request again, since the client clearly never saw the first result
Return 409 Conflict, since that key has already been used by an earlier request
Return 204 No Content, since there is nothing new for the server to process now
questions.why: The server saves the key with the status and body of the first result, and a retry gets that same response, so the client learns the outcome without a second charge. A 409 or 204 leaves the client unsure whether the first attempt worked. Keys are kept for a bounded period, often 24 hours.
questions.asked: Goes past the definition to the implementation; payment-adjacent roles ask this almost every time.

questions.q: A client reuses an idempotency key from a payment it made an hour ago, but with a different amount. How should the server respond?
choices: Process it as new, since the body differs, which makes it a new request
Return the stored response from the first payment, ignoring the new body
Reject it with an error, since one key must always mean the same request
Update yesterday's payment to the new amount, since the key identifies it
questions.why: Store a hash of the request with the key; a mismatch means a client bug, and silently replaying the old response or charging again both hide it (Stripe, for example, returns an error). Keys are also scoped per account, so two customers generating the same key never collide.
questions.asked: Edge cases are where idempotency implementations go wrong; this one checks you store more than the key.

questions.q: Two requests with the same idempotency key arrive within milliseconds, before either has finished. How do you stop both from executing?
choices: Check whether a stored response exists for the key before starting the work
Rely on the client, since well-behaved clients never retry until they time out
Compare the two request timestamps and keep only the earlier of the pair
Claim the key first with a unique insert; the loser gets a 409 or waits
questions.why: Check-then-act is a race: both requests see no stored response and both proceed. Insert the key in an 'in progress' state under a unique constraint (or take a lock) before doing the work, so exactly one wins; the other gets 409 and retries later, or waits for the result. Then fill in the response when done.
questions.asked: The concurrency case is what separates a toy idempotency layer from a real one.

questions.q: This Express webhook handler rejects some genuine provider events as having a bad signature. Why?
choices: HMAC-SHA256 output differs between Node versions, so it must be pinned
The signature covers the raw bytes, and re-serialised JSON can differ
Express lowercases header values, so the signature no longer matches
`express.json()` strips unknown fields that were part of the signature
questions.why: The provider signed the exact bytes it sent. Parsing and `JSON.stringify` change whitespace, key escaping and numbers (`1.0` becomes `1`), so the hash differs. Capture the raw body for this route (`express.raw({ type: 'application/json' })`), verify over it, then parse. Express does not alter header values or drop fields.
questions.asked: A real integration bug; the fix shows you know what an HMAC actually covers.

questions.q: Your webhook endpoint verifies an HMAC signature. What stops an attacker who captured one genuine request from replaying it tomorrow?
choices: Nothing is needed, since a valid HMAC can only be produced by the provider
Requiring HTTPS, since TLS rejects the same request being sent twice
Rotating the shared secret after every event that the endpoint receives
A signed timestamp checked against a window, plus remembering event ids
questions.why: A replayed request carries a perfectly valid signature. Providers include a timestamp in the signed payload, so you reject anything older than a few minutes, and storing processed event ids makes the handler idempotent against replays and duplicate deliveries inside the window. TLS protects the channel, not against resending captured contents.
questions.asked: A signature alone is the common answer; interviewers want the timestamp window and dedupe.

questions.q: In Node 24, what is wrong with comparing a webhook signature this way, and what replaces it?
choices: It leaks timing; compare equal-length buffers with `crypto.timingSafeEqual`
`===` coerces types; use `Object.is` so the strings compare strictly
Hex is case-sensitive; lowercase both strings, and then `===` is safe
It is correct, as string comparison in V8 always takes a constant time
questions.why: String equality returns at the first differing character, so response times can leak how many leading bytes of a guess were right. `crypto.timingSafeEqual` takes the same time for any input, but throws `ERR_CRYPTO_TIMING_SAFE_EQUAL_LENGTH` if the buffers differ in length, so check lengths first. `Object.is` short-circuits just the same.
questions.asked: A small detail that signals security care; the length-check follow-up catches people who have only read about it.

questions.q: Why does an API cap request body size, typically at 100 KB to a few MB for JSON routes?
choices: Because HTTP/1.1 itself forbids bodies larger than a few megabytes
So that one client cannot exhaust memory and CPU with a huge payload
Because JSON parsers are only able to handle files up to about 1 MB
So that the browser can compress bodies before they reach the server
questions.why: A body parser buffers and parses the whole payload before your code runs, so an unbounded body is a cheap denial of service: memory, CPU and event-loop time for one request. HTTP sets no such limit. Raise the cap only on routes that need it, such as uploads, which should stream to storage instead.
questions.asked: Asks for the reason behind a default everyone copies; strong answers mention per-route limits for uploads.

questions.q: Where should an API validate the shape of incoming JSON, such as types, required fields and lengths?
choices: In the database only, since constraints there are the final line of defence
In the frontend form, since that is where users type the values in the end
At the boundary, with a schema, before the data reaches any business logic
Deep in each service method, right before a field is first actually used
questions.why: Validate once at the edge (a schema library such as zod, or model validation in ASP.NET Core) and reject bad input with a 400, so everything inside can rely on typed, bounded data. Frontend checks are for UX and can be bypassed; database constraints are a backstop that returns poor errors; scattered checks get forgotten.
questions.asked: A fundamentals check; strong candidates add that unknown fields should be rejected or stripped.

questions.q: An API that uses cookie sessions sets these CORS headers on every response. What is the risk?
choices: None, since echoing the Origin is how CORS is meant to allow a caller
Browsers reject it, because Origin must be `*` whenever credentials are sent
Any website can call the API with the user's cookies and read the reply
Only same-site pages can now call it, which breaks the partner integrations
questions.why: Reflecting whatever Origin arrives, together with credentials, tells the browser that every site is trusted, so evil.example can fetch the victim's data with their cookies and read it. Check the Origin against an explicit allowlist. The browser does refuse `*` with credentials, which is exactly why people reflect the Origin to get around it. Chrome's SameSite=Lax default only blunts this when the session cookie is not `SameSite=None`, and a cross-site SPA needs None anyway; Firefox and Safari do not default to Lax.
questions.asked: CORS misconfiguration is a common pentest finding; this checks you see CORS as an access-control surface, not a nuisance to silence.

questions.q: Besides answering 429 when a client is over its limit, why do APIs send `RateLimit-Remaining` and `RateLimit-Reset` (or the older `X-RateLimit-*` forms) on every successful response?
choices: So a well-behaved client can pace itself and stop before it is rejected, instead of learning the limit only from 429s
So the browser can throttle `fetch` automatically, since it reads those headers and queues requests that would exceed the quota
So CDNs can cache the response for exactly the reset interval, which replaces `Cache-Control` on rate-limited routes
So the server can skip its own counter on the next request, since the client echoes the remaining value back in a header
questions.why: The headers are advisory: a client that reads `RateLimit-Remaining` can spread a batch across the window rather than hammering until a 429, and its rejected retries stop counting against it. Browsers and CDNs do nothing with them, and the server never trusts a client-reported count. The names are still an IETF draft, so document which form you send and serve them from the same shared counter on every instance.
questions.asked: Shows you treat a rate limit as a contract with the client rather than a wall, and that you know the headers are advisory.

questions.q: This Express 5 route checks that the account belongs to the caller. Which object-level authorization hole remains?
choices: The statement is loaded by id alone, so any statement id works under your account
The account lookup should return 403 rather than 404 when the owner does not match
The ownership check should run in a separate middleware before the handler is called
The two route parameters should be parsed as integers before either query runs
questions.why: The parent check proves the account is yours, but the statement is fetched without `accountId`, so `/accounts/<mine>/statements/<yours>` returns your data. Scope the child query to the checked parent (`{ id, accountId }`). Moving the check into middleware or parsing ids changes nothing about which statement is returned.
questions.asked: Nested routes are where BOLA hides in real code reviews; a strong answer scopes every query, not just the first one.

questions.q: A user requests `GET /api/orders/981`, which exists but belongs to another customer. Why do many APIs answer 404 rather than 403?
choices: A 403 would make the browser drop the session cookie and log the user out entirely
404 does not confirm the order exists, so ids cannot be probed to learn what is real
403 is reserved for authentication failures and must carry a WWW-Authenticate header
Caches store 403 responses for all users, while 404s are never cached by any proxy
questions.why: Answering 403 tells an attacker the id is valid and someone else's, which leaks existence and helps enumeration; 404 treats 'not yours' like 'not there'. 403 is fine when existence is not secret, such as a role-gated admin page. It is 401, not 403, that pairs with `WWW-Authenticate`, and neither status touches cookies.
questions.asked: Shows you think about information disclosure; a strong answer says when 403 is still the honest choice.

questions.q: In an ASP.NET Core 9 API, a teammate binds the request straight to the EF Core entity. What is the security problem?
choices: Minimal APIs cannot bind entity classes, so every request fails with a 415 response
`Update` marks every property modified, so clients can set `IsAdmin` or `Balance`
Setting `Id` from the claims principal lets a client overwrite some other user's row
EF Core refuses to save an entity that was not first loaded by the same `DbContext`
questions.why: Binding to the entity makes every mapped property writable from JSON, and `Update` saves them all: that is mass assignment. Bind to a request DTO with only the editable fields and copy them onto the loaded entity. Taking the id from the claims is the right move, and EF Core happily attaches a detached entity.
questions.asked: Over-posting in .NET is a classic review finding; interviewers want to hear 'request DTO', not '[Bind] attributes'.

questions.q: `GET /api/orders/7` returns the order with `Include(o => o.Customer)` serialised as-is. Why is this a data-exposure risk even when the caller owns the order?
choices: The customer entity may carry fields such as `PasswordHash` that now leave the API
Loading the related customer turns the single order query into an N+1 query loop
Serialising navigation properties always throws a cycle error in System.Text.Json
Order owners must never see any customer data, including their own name or email
questions.why: Serialising entities means every column of every included relation goes over the wire, so internal fields leak as the model grows. Project to a response DTO that names exactly what the client needs. One `Include` is a join, not N+1, and cycles are a separate serialisation concern that `ReferenceHandler` can handle.
questions.asked: Checks that you shape responses deliberately instead of trusting the entity graph.

questions.q: Admin endpoints live under `/api/internal-7f3k/` and are not linked from the UI, but only check that the caller is logged in. What is wrong?
choices: Nothing, since an unguessable path prefix works in the same way as a secret key
Only that the prefix should be rotated regularly, the way API keys are rotated
Paths leak through bundles, logs and proxies; each route still needs a role check
The routes should move to a separate port, which browsers are not able to reach
questions.why: A hidden path is obscurity, not authorization: it appears in JavaScript bundles, browser history, proxy logs and referrers, and once known anyone logged in can call it. Enforce a role or permission policy on the whole admin group. A different port is equally reachable by curl.
questions.asked: Tests whether you recognise function-level authorization gaps dressed up as secrecy.

questions.q: An Express router applies `requireAdmin` with `router.get('/users/:id', requireAdmin, ...)` and registers `router.put('/users/:id', handler)` separately. What does a security reviewer flag?
choices: The GET handler should also be open, since reading a user record is harmless
Express 5 applies route middleware to every method on a path, so both are safe
`requireAdmin` must be registered after the handler for it to run on responses
The PUT route has no admin check, so any caller can modify a user's record
questions.why: Middleware passed to `router.get` runs only for GET; the PUT on the same path is unprotected. Attach the guard with `router.use` on the admin router or to each route, and test each method. Express never shares per-route middleware across methods.
questions.asked: Method-by-method gaps are a real BFLA pattern; strong candidates protect the router, not individual handlers.

questions.q: Your 'forgot password' endpoint sends an SMS through a paid provider, is unauthenticated, and has no limits. Which risk does OWASP API4 (unrestricted resource consumption) highlight here?
choices: An attacker can read other users' reset codes by guessing the SMS message ids
Scripts can trigger thousands of paid messages, running up your provider's bill
The provider will refuse to deliver messages to numbers outside the user's country
Unauthenticated endpoints cannot call third-party APIs from a production server
questions.why: API4 covers cost as well as CPU: each call spends money on SMS, email or AI APIs, so abuse becomes 'SMS pumping' fraud. Limit per phone number, per IP and per account, cap daily spend at the provider, and add a challenge for anonymous flows. Guessing message ids is not the risk the endpoint creates.
questions.asked: Interviewers like candidates who see money, not just CPU, as a resource an API can exhaust.

questions.q: Bots buy every ticket in a limited sale within seconds using valid accounts and normal-looking requests. Which OWASP API risk is this, and what kind of fix helps?
choices: Broken authentication; force every buyer to log in again before checkout opens
Security misconfiguration; move the sale endpoint behind a web application firewall
Broken object-level authorization; check that each ticket id belongs to the buyer
Unrestricted access to a business flow; add per-account caps and bot detection
questions.why: Every request is individually valid, so the problem is automated abuse of a sensitive flow (API6). Fixes are business-level: purchase limits per account and card, device or behaviour signals, queues and challenges. A WAF or re-login does not stop a legitimate-looking bot account.
questions.asked: API6 is the least intuitive entry; strong answers talk about the business rule, not just the HTTP layer.

questions.q: A 'link preview' endpoint fetches any URL the user submits and returns the page title. What will an attacker try first?
choices: `http://169.254.169.254/` or `http://localhost:6379`, to reach internal services
`javascript:alert(1)` URLs, to run script inside your server's Node process
A very long URL, to overflow the buffer that holds the address in V8 memory
An `https` URL with an expired certificate, to break TLS for other users
questions.why: Server-side request forgery makes your server a proxy into its own network: cloud metadata endpoints, admin panels and databases that trust internal traffic. Resolve the host, block private and link-local ranges, allow only http/https, and ideally fetch from an isolated egress. A `javascript:` URL is not executed by an HTTP client.
questions.asked: SSRF is on every API security checklist; naming the cloud metadata address shows real-world awareness.

questions.q: Your SSRF guard resolves the hostname, checks the IP is public, then calls `fetch(url)`. How can an attacker still reach `127.0.0.1`?
choices: By encoding the hostname in punycode so that the resolver skips the check
By sending the request over HTTP/2, which bypasses DNS resolution entirely
By using DNS rebinding: a short TTL answers public first, internal second
By adding a port number, since the guard only validates port 80 and 443
questions.why: `fetch` resolves the name again, and a hostile DNS server with TTL 0 can return a public IP for your check and `127.0.0.1` for the real connection. Pin the resolved address: connect to the IP you validated (a custom lookup or agent), or route through an egress proxy that enforces the rule. HTTP/2 still resolves DNS.
questions.asked: A deep follow-up that separates people who have implemented SSRF defences from people who have read about them.

questions.q: An SSRF filter validates the submitted URL, then fetches it with the client's default settings. Which setting most often reopens the hole?
choices: Keep-alive, since a reused socket can point at a different host than validated
Automatic redirects, since a public URL can answer 302 to an internal address
Response decompression, since a gzip body can contain an internal hostname
The default timeout, since a slow host is retried against a private address
questions.why: Most HTTP clients follow redirects by default, so the validated public URL just redirects to `http://10.0.0.5/admin`. Disable automatic redirects (`redirect: 'manual'` in fetch) and validate each hop yourself, or cap and re-check them. Keep-alive sockets stay bound to their original host.
questions.asked: Tests whether you know the classic bypass; strong candidates mention validating every hop.

questions.q: A production API returns full .NET exception stack traces in 500 responses. Which OWASP API category covers this, and what is the fix?
choices: Unsafe consumption of APIs; wrap every call to the database in its own try/catch
Broken authentication; require a login before anyone can trigger a server error
Improper inventory management; document every possible exception in OpenAPI
Security misconfiguration; return a generic problem body and log the details
questions.why: Stack traces reveal frameworks, versions, file paths and sometimes SQL, which is misconfiguration (API8). In ASP.NET Core, the developer exception page must stay development-only; production returns a generic problem details body with a trace id you can find in the logs. Hiding errors behind login does not stop logged-in attackers.
questions.asked: Basic, but interviewers listen for 'log it, correlate it, don't return it'.

questions.q: You fixed a BOLA bug in `/v2/invoices/:id`, but `/v1/invoices/:id` still runs the old handler for 'legacy clients'. Which OWASP API risk does that leave?
choices: Improper inventory management: forgotten versions keep old flaws exposed
Server-side request forgery, since v1 can be used to proxy calls into v2
Unsafe consumption of APIs, since v1 clients send unvalidated JSON payloads
Broken function-level authorization, since v1 lacks an administrator role
questions.why: API9 is about not knowing, or not retiring, what you run: old versions, debug routes and staging hosts. Attackers enumerate `/v1` because fixes land only in the newest code. Keep an inventory, apply fixes to every live version, and sunset old ones on a schedule.
questions.asked: Checks that you think about the whole API surface, not only the code you are currently editing.

questions.q: A `staging-api.example.com` host runs last month's build against a copy of production data and is reachable from the internet. Why is it a serious finding?
choices: Staging hosts are indexed by search engines, which lowers the main site's rank
It holds real data behind older, less-watched code and usually weaker settings
Running two versions at once causes EF Core migrations to conflict at startup
Browsers block cookies from any subdomain that shares data with production
questions.why: Non-production environments often have debug settings, stale dependencies and fewer monitors, yet a production data copy makes them just as valuable to attack. Keep staging private (VPN or IP allowlist) and use anonymised or synthetic data. This is improper inventory and misconfiguration together.
questions.asked: A realistic breach pattern; strong answers mention both network isolation and anonymised data.

questions.q: Attackers try leaked email/password pairs from other sites against your `/api/login`, a few per account from many IPs. What is this attack called, and which defence targets it best?
choices: Brute force; require passwords of at least 16 characters on the next login
Session fixation; issue a fresh session identifier after every successful login
Credential stuffing; add breached-password checks, MFA and per-account limits
Password spraying; lock every account for 24 hours after its first failed login
questions.why: Credential stuffing reuses real pairs, so password rules do nothing and per-IP limits miss a botnet. Check passwords against breach lists (as NIST 800-63B recommends), offer MFA, and throttle per account with care. Hard lockouts after one failure let attackers lock out every user.
questions.asked: Tests whether you can name the attack and pick defences that match it rather than a generic 'rate limit'.

questions.q: A password-reset flow emails a link containing a token. Which token design is correct?
choices: A signed JWT holding the user id, valid for 7 days so slow users can finish
The user's id encrypted with AES, so that only the server can read it back
A random value, stored hashed, valid about an hour and deleted when first used
A hash of the user's email and current time, so it can be recomputed later
questions.why: A reset token must be unguessable, short-lived and single-use, and storing only its hash means a database leak does not hand out live reset links. A long-lived JWT cannot be revoked once used, and an email-plus-timestamp hash is predictable if the attacker knows roughly when it was issued.
questions.asked: Reset flows are a common take-home review item; strong answers mention single use and hashing at rest.

questions.q: Your login API returns 'No account with that email' or 'Wrong password' depending on the failure. What is the problem?
choices: It breaks RFC 9457, which requires one fixed `title` string for each status code
It lets attackers confirm which emails are registered before guessing passwords
It prevents the browser's password manager from offering to update saved logins
It should return 404 for the unknown email, and 401 only for the wrong password
questions.why: Distinct messages enable user enumeration, which feeds credential stuffing and phishing. Return one generic 'invalid email or password' for both, and make signup and reset flows equally quiet (for example, 'if an account exists, we've sent an email'). Returning 404 versus 401 leaks the same fact through the status.
questions.asked: A quick check for security instinct; good candidates extend it to signup and password reset.

questions.q: Your login handler returns immediately when the email is unknown, but runs Argon2id (about 200 ms) when it exists. Both paths return the same message. What still leaks?
choices: The unknown-email path skips the audit log, which an attacker can observe later
Argon2id output differs by platform, so the response size reveals the server OS
Nothing leaks, because both responses carry an identical status code and body
Response time: fast replies mark unregistered emails, so accounts can be listed
questions.why: A timing side channel: 5 ms versus 200 ms is easy to measure over many requests, so enumeration is still possible. Verify against a dummy hash when the user does not exist so both paths do the same work. Identical bodies fix only the visible channel.
questions.asked: A deep follow-up to the enumeration question; mentioning the dummy-hash fix is what interviewers want.

questions.q: A partner integration passes its API key as `GET /api/orders?api_key=sk_live_...`. Why ask them to move it to a header?
choices: Query strings are capped at 256 characters, so long keys are cut off in transit
HTTPS encrypts headers but sends the query string of every request in plain text
Headers are compressed with HPACK, which makes the key unreadable to proxies
URLs are written to access logs, proxy logs and monitoring tools, leaking the key
questions.why: The whole URL is recorded by web servers, load balancers, APM tools and sometimes browser history, so secrets in query strings end up in many places. Send keys in `Authorization` or a dedicated header, which logs normally omit. TLS encrypts the path and query too, so the issue is logging, not the wire.
questions.asked: Shows you know where secrets actually leak; strong candidates mention log redaction as a second layer.

questions.q: A customer needs to rotate an API key without downtime. What should your API support?
choices: Two active keys per client, so the new one is deployed before the old is revoked
Keys that change automatically at midnight UTC, with the new one emailed ahead
A single key that stays valid for 24 hours after the replacement is generated
Rotation only by support ticket, so an engineer can check nothing will break
questions.why: Overlapping validity lets the client ship the new key everywhere, confirm traffic has moved (show 'last used' per key), then revoke the old one. A fixed grace window may be too short for a real rollout, and scheduled automatic rotation breaks clients that miss the email.
questions.asked: Operational key management separates people who have run an API from people who have only called one.

questions.q: Your public GraphQL API has introspection enabled in production. What is the usual guidance?
choices: Keep it enabled, because disabling it makes queries return partial data only
Disable it for public clients; it maps the whole schema for attackers at once
Disable it, which fully secures resolvers that lack authorization checks
Keep it enabled, since GraphQL servers refuse queries without a schema fetch
questions.why: Introspection hands out every type, field and mutation, including ones the UI never uses. Turning it off for public clients (keeping it in dev or behind auth) removes a free map, but it is not a control: every resolver still needs authorization, because field names can be guessed or leaked from the client bundle.
questions.asked: Tests whether you treat introspection as defence in depth rather than a fix.

questions.q: A client sends a GraphQL query nesting `friends { friends { friends { ... } } }` twenty levels deep. What protects the server?
choices: A request body size limit, since deeply nested queries are always very large
HTTP/2 multiplexing, which spreads each nested level over separate streams
Query depth and cost limits checked before any resolver is allowed to run
A timeout on the database connection, which cancels the query after 30 seconds
questions.why: A short query can fan out to millions of resolver calls, so body size says little about cost. Validate depth and estimated complexity before execution, and use persisted queries for first-party clients. A database timeout fires only after the damage is done.
questions.asked: GraphQL-specific resource exhaustion is a standard follow-up once you say you have used GraphQL.

questions.q: Your GraphQL `login` mutation is limited to 10 HTTP requests per minute per IP. How can an attacker still try 1,000 passwords a minute?
choices: By sending the mutation over a WebSocket subscription, which has no limits
By using aliases to put 100 `login` calls in each single HTTP request
By using introspection to find a second, unlimited login mutation
By switching the request to GET, which rate limiters do not count
questions.why: Aliases (`a1: login(...) a2: login(...)`) run many operations in one request, so per-request limits undercount. Count operations or attempts per account, cap aliases and batch size, and rate-limit at the resolver for sensitive mutations. GET versus POST does not matter to a limiter keyed on requests.
questions.asked: Batching attacks are a known GraphQL pitfall; strong candidates limit per operation, not per HTTP request.

questions.q: Where should object-level authorization checks live in a typical layered Express or ASP.NET Core CRUD API?
choices: In the React app, which hides records the user may not see before rendering
In a single global middleware that inspects every URL for id segments
In the database connection string, using one login per application user
Next to the data access for each operation, scoping queries to the caller
questions.why: Only the code that loads a record knows which record it is and how ownership is modelled, so scope queries (`WHERE owner_id = @me`) or call an authorization service per operation; ASP.NET Core resource-based `IAuthorizationService` fits here. URL-parsing middleware breaks on nested or body-supplied ids, and UI hiding is not a control.
questions.asked: Tests whether you have an architecture for authorization, not just a list of checks.

questions.q: A `POST /api/orders` body includes `"unitPrice": 0.01` that the React checkout copies from the product page. What should the server do with it?
choices: Accept it if it matches the price that was shown on the page within the last hour
Accept it but log a warning whenever it differs from the price in the catalogue
Ignore it and load the price from its own catalogue when creating the order
Reject the request with 400 whenever the body contains any numeric field
questions.why: Anything the client sends can be edited, so prices, discounts and totals must come from server-side data. The body should carry only what the user chooses (product id, quantity, coupon code). A 'recently shown' price still trusts the client, and logging a warning leaves the order underpriced.
questions.asked: A classic trust-boundary question; the strong answer lists which fields the client may choose.

questions.q: A token bucket holds at most 10 tokens and refills at 1 token per second. A client has been idle for a minute, then fires 15 requests at once. Roughly how many succeed immediately?
choices: 15, because a minute of idling has banked 60 tokens for the client to spend
10, because the bucket is capped at its capacity however long the client idled
1, because a token bucket only ever releases one request per refill interval
0, because a burst above capacity empties the bucket and blocks the whole batch
questions.why: Capacity sets the maximum burst and the refill rate sets the sustained rate, so tokens stop accumulating at 10. The first 10 requests pass and the rest wait for refills or get 429. Releasing one request per interval describes a leaky bucket, which smooths output instead of allowing bursts.
questions.asked: Checks that you understand burst versus sustained rate, the point of choosing a token bucket.

questions.q: A sliding-window-counter limiter allows 100 requests per minute. The previous minute had 80 requests, the current minute has 30 so far, and you are 15 seconds into it. Is the next request allowed?
choices: No; 80 + 30 = 110 is over the limit, so it is refused until the next minute
Yes; only the 30 requests in the current minute count, well under the limit
Yes; the estimate is 80 × 0.75 + 30 = 90, which is still under the limit
No; the estimate is 80 × 0.25 + 30 = 50 per quarter, over the 25 allowed
questions.why: The counter weights the previous window by how much of it still overlaps the sliding window: 45 of 60 seconds, so 0.75 × 80 + 30 = 90. It approximates a sliding log with two counters per key instead of a timestamp per request. Counting only the current minute is the fixed-window behaviour that allows double bursts at the boundary.
questions.asked: A deep-dive question for anyone who claims to have built a limiter; the arithmetic shows you know the trade-off.

questions.q: An Express 5 API behind one load balancer rate-limits by `req.ip`. Why is this setting dangerous?
questions.code:
app.set('trust proxy', true);
app.use(rateLimit({ windowMs: 60_000, limit: 100 }));
choices: `true` makes `req.ip` the balancer's address, so all users share one counter
`true` disables the limiter for proxied requests, so no one is ever limited
`true` trusts every `X-Forwarded-For` entry, so a client can spoof its own IP
`true` makes Express ignore IPv6 clients, so they bypass the rate limiter
questions.why: With `trust proxy` set to `true`, Express takes the left-most `X-Forwarded-For` value, which the client controls, so each request can claim a new IP and dodge the limit. Set it to the number of trusted hops (here `1`) or the proxy's addresses so `req.ip` is what your balancer saw. Setting it to `false` is what collapses everyone onto the balancer's IP.
questions.asked: A real-world misconfiguration; strong candidates know exactly which header value the setting trusts.

questions.q: A Redis limiter runs `INCR key`, then, if the result is 1, `EXPIRE key 60`, as two separate commands. What can go wrong?
choices: INCR resets the key's TTL each time, so the window keeps sliding forward forever
If the process dies between the two calls, the key never expires and stays blocked
EXPIRE on an existing key throws an error, so the second request always fails
Two INCRs from different servers can both return 1, doubling the allowed limit
questions.why: A crash or timeout after INCR leaves a counter with no TTL, so that user is limited permanently once it passes the cap. Make it atomic with a Lua script, `SET key 0 EX 60 NX` followed by INCR, or a MULTI transaction. INCR is atomic, so two servers never both see 1, and it does not touch the TTL.
questions.asked: Distributed limiting questions reward people who think about partial failure between steps.

questions.q: What is the difference between a rate limit and a quota in an API product?
choices: A rate limit applies only to anonymous users; quotas apply to logged-in users
A rate limit is enforced by the CDN; a quota is enforced inside the database
A rate limit counts bytes transferred; a quota counts the number of requests
A rate limit caps short bursts; a quota caps total usage over a billing period
questions.why: Rate limits protect the service from spikes (100 per minute), while quotas enforce plan allowances (50,000 per month) and usually map to billing. They answer differently too: a rate limit says 'retry in 20 s', a quota says 'upgrade or wait until the period resets'. Both can count requests or other units, wherever they are enforced.
questions.asked: A simple product-thinking check; strong answers mention the different client messages.

questions.q: You add `builder.Services.AddRateLimiter(...)` and `app.UseRateLimiter()` in ASP.NET Core 9. Rejected clients receive 503 instead of 429. Why?
choices: `RejectionStatusCode` defaults to 503, so you must set it to 429 yourself
429 is only sent when the limiter is registered before `UseRouting()`
Kestrel converts 429 to 503 unless HTTP/2 is enabled on the endpoint
The fixed-window limiter returns 503; only the token bucket returns 429
questions.why: The built-in middleware's `RateLimiterOptions.RejectionStatusCode` is 503 by default; set `options.RejectionStatusCode = StatusCodes.Status429TooManyRequests` and consider `OnRejected` to add `Retry-After`. The status does not depend on middleware order or the algorithm chosen.
questions.asked: A small framework detail that shows you have actually shipped the .NET rate limiter.

questions.q: A CSV export endpoint takes about 20 seconds and a lot of memory per call. Which limit protects the server best?
choices: A fixed window of 60 requests per minute per user, applied at the gateway
A concurrency limit, such as two in-flight exports per user and 10 overall
A token bucket with a large burst size, so that users can export in batches
A request body size limit, since exports are triggered by a large POST body
questions.why: The cost here is time held, not request count: 60 per minute of a 20-second job means up to 20 running at once per user. A concurrency limiter caps work in progress (`AddConcurrencyLimiter` in ASP.NET Core, a semaphore or queue in Node). Moving the export to a background job with 202 is often the real fix.
questions.asked: Tests whether you pick the limiter to fit the resource instead of reaching for requests-per-minute every time.

questions.q: After an outage, 5,000 clients retry with the same exponential backoff: 1 s, 2 s, 4 s. Why do guides say to add random jitter?
choices: Jitter shortens the average wait, so clients recover sooner after the outage ends
Without jitter, the backoff doubles too slowly to give the server time to recover
Without jitter, the clients stay in sync and hit the server in synchronised waves
Jitter is needed only for WebSocket reconnects; HTTP clients never synchronise
questions.why: Clients that failed together retry together, so each backoff step becomes a spike that knocks the recovering service over again. Randomising the delay (for example 'full jitter', a random value between 0 and the backoff) spreads the load. Jitter does not change how fast the delay grows.
questions.asked: Thundering herds come up in system-design rounds; naming full jitter is a plus.

questions.q: Why is rate limiting usually applied at the gateway or early in the middleware pipeline, rather than inside each handler?
choices: So rejected requests cost almost nothing, before auth, parsing or database work
Because handlers cannot return 429, which only middleware is allowed to produce
Because limits enforced after authentication cannot see which user made the call
So that the limit applies to static files, which is its main purpose on an API
questions.why: The point is to shed load cheaply; if every request still parses a body, hits the database and runs business logic before being refused, the limiter protects little. Per-user limits still need identity, so they sit just after authentication, and handlers can return 429 perfectly well.
questions.asked: A placement question that shows you understand what a limiter is protecting.

questions.q: Your API stores idempotency keys so it can replay results. Which record per key supports correct behaviour?
choices: The key alone, so that any repeat is rejected with 409 without re-running it
The key and the created resource's id, so that repeats return a fresh 201
The key and the response body only, since the status can be inferred later
The client id, a hash of the request, and the stored status and body to replay
questions.why: Scoping by client stops collisions across customers, the request hash detects a reused key with a different body (which should be refused), and the stored status and body let a retry get the identical answer. Rejecting every repeat with 409 breaks the whole point: the client retried because it never saw the first answer.
questions.asked: Tests whether you have designed the storage, not just heard of the header.

questions.q: Why is an idempotency key generated by the client rather than returned by the server?
choices: Servers cannot generate random values that are unique enough across instances
The key must exist before the first attempt so that every retry can reuse it
Client-generated keys let the server skip authentication on retried requests
Keys from the server would have to be signed, which slows down every request
questions.why: The risky case is a request whose response was lost; if the server issued the key in that response, the client would never have it. The client creates a UUID per logical operation, stores it with the pending action, and sends it on each retry. Idempotency never replaces authentication.
questions.asked: A quick reasoning check on why the design works; good candidates mention persisting the key with the pending action.

questions.q: Two different customers happen to send the same `Idempotency-Key` value to `POST /payments`. What should a well-designed API do?
choices: Replay the first customer's stored response to the second, since the keys match
Reject the second request with 409, since each key must be unique across the API
Treat them separately, because stored keys are scoped to the authenticated client
Merge the two payments into one, since the provider sees a single idempotent call
questions.why: Keys are namespaced by account or API key, so one client's key never collides with another's; replaying across clients would even leak another customer's response. A global uniqueness rule forces clients to coordinate on something only they control.
questions.asked: Surfaces whether you see the data-leak angle of a naive global key store.

questions.q: A mobile app creates orders offline and syncs later. Which design makes creation naturally idempotent without an `Idempotency-Key` header?
choices: The client generates the order's UUID and sends `PUT /orders/{id}` with the body
The client sends `POST /orders` and deletes duplicates found in a nightly job
The server sets a unique index on `createdAt`, rejecting a second identical insert
The client sends `GET /orders/create?...` so that browser caches absorb retries
questions.why: With a client-chosen id, creation is a PUT to a known URL: repeating it leaves one order, and the server can return 201 first and 200 after. A timestamp index rejects legitimate distinct orders made in the same instant, and nightly cleanup means duplicates were charged and shipped first.
questions.asked: Shows you can design idempotency into resource identity, a useful alternative to a key store.

questions.q: Payment providers deliver webhooks 'at least once'. What must your handler do because of that?
choices: Return 500 on the first delivery so that the provider sends a confirming copy
Record each event id and skip events that have already been processed
Process every event twice so that the result matches the provider's count
Verify the signature only on the first delivery and trust any later copies
questions.why: At-least-once means duplicates are normal (after timeouts, retries or provider incidents), so the consumer must be idempotent: store processed event ids with a unique constraint, or make the effect itself idempotent. Every delivery still needs signature verification, because copies can be forged too.
questions.asked: Webhook dedupe is table stakes; strong answers mention the unique constraint doing the work.

questions.q: Your app receives `subscription.updated` before the matching `subscription.created` webhook. What is a robust way to handle ordering?
choices: Reject any event whose predecessor is missing and ask the provider to resend
Sort events by their arrival time on your server and apply them in that order
Buffer every event for ten minutes, then apply that batch in id order at once
Treat the event as a signal and fetch the object's current state from the API
questions.why: Providers do not guarantee order, so applying payloads in arrival order can roll state backwards. Re-fetching the current object (or comparing a version or `updated` timestamp and ignoring older ones) converges on the truth. Arrival order is exactly what is unreliable, and fixed buffering still misorders late events.
questions.asked: Out-of-order delivery is the follow-up after dedupe; the 'fetch current state' answer is what interviewers want.

questions.q: You are building outgoing webhooks for your own customers. What should each delivery include so receivers can trust it?
choices: The customer's API key in a header, so the receiver can compare it with its own
A JWT signed with your TLS private key, so receivers can verify it with your cert
An HMAC of the timestamp and raw body using a per-endpoint secret, plus an event id
An IP allowlist in the payload, so the receiver can check where it came from
questions.why: A per-endpoint signing secret, a signed timestamp and a unique event id let receivers check authenticity, reject replays and dedupe; the Standard Webhooks spec formalises this. Sending the customer's own API key over the wire leaks a credential, and reusing a TLS key for application signing mixes purposes.
questions.asked: Flips the usual webhook question; strong candidates mention per-endpoint secrets and rotation.

questions.q: A webhook endpoint authenticates the sender only by checking that the source IP is on the provider's published list. What is the weakness?
choices: Providers' IP ranges change daily, so an allowlist blocks every real delivery
IP checks work only for IPv4, while webhook senders deliver over IPv6 by default
Behind a proxy the IP may come from a spoofable header, and the body is unsigned
IP allowlists force the provider to send webhooks over plain HTTP, not HTTPS
questions.why: Proxies often mean trusting `X-Forwarded-For`, which can be forged if misconfigured, and shared cloud ranges may be rentable by attackers; nothing proves the body is unmodified. Use the signature as the primary check and treat IP filtering as an extra layer. Published ranges change occasionally, not daily.
questions.asked: Tests defence-in-depth thinking; the answer is 'signature first, IPs second'.

questions.q: An API authenticated by session cookie accepts `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` on `POST /api/transfer`, and its CORS policy allows only your own origin. Why is it still exposed to CSRF?
choices: A cross-site HTML form can POST that type with no preflight; CORS never blocks it
Form-encoded bodies skip TLS, so an attacker on the network can change the amount
CORS policies apply only to GET requests, so every POST is allowed by default
Browsers attach cookies to form posts only when the API also allows credentials
questions.why: CORS controls whether a page can read the response, not whether a simple request is sent; a form POST with a simple content type goes out, cookies may ride along, and the transfer runs. Require JSON (which forces a preflight), use SameSite cookies and CSRF tokens. The body encoding has nothing to do with TLS.
questions.asked: The classic 'CORS is not CSRF protection' question; strong answers say what CORS actually blocks.

questions.q: Your session cookie is `SameSite=Lax`. Which CSRF risk remains?
choices: Cross-site `fetch` POSTs from any page still send the cookie automatically
Top-level cross-site form POSTs still send the cookie on the first request
Lax cookies are sent to every subdomain of any site the user visits later
GET endpoints with side effects, and attacks from sibling subdomains
questions.why: Lax sends the cookie on top-level GET navigations, so a state-changing GET is still forgeable, and 'site' means registrable domain, so a compromised `blog.example.com` is same-site with `app.example.com`. Lax withholds the cookie on cross-site POSTs, form or fetch. Keep GETs safe and add CSRF tokens for defence in depth.
questions.asked: A deep follow-up: interviewers want the 'same-site vs same-origin' distinction.

questions.q: Why is an API that reads its token only from the `Authorization: Bearer` header not vulnerable to classic CSRF?
choices: Bearer tokens are encrypted, so an attacker's page cannot read or change them
Browsers never attach that header automatically; your own JavaScript must add it
Preflight requests always fail for cross-site pages that send an `Authorization` header
Bearer tokens expire within minutes, well before a CSRF attack could be staged
questions.why: CSRF exploits credentials the browser adds on its own, such as cookies; a header set by your code is not sent by a forged form or image tag. The trade-off is that the token lives where JavaScript can reach it, so XSS becomes the bigger risk. Bearer tokens are usually signed, not encrypted.
questions.asked: Checks that you understand why CSRF happens rather than memorising 'use tokens'.

questions.q: An API's CORS allowlist includes the origin `null` so that a local HTML file can call it during testing, with credentials allowed. Why is that risky in production?
choices: `null` makes the browser skip the preflight, so every method is allowed
Any site can send `Origin: null` from a sandboxed iframe and read responses
`null` matches every origin, so it is the same as returning `*` with cookies
Browsers reject `null` in the header, so the whole CORS policy stops working
questions.why: Sandboxed iframes, `data:` URLs and some redirects send `Origin: null`, so an attacker's page can produce it on purpose and, with credentials allowed, read the user's data. Never allow `null`; test with a real local origin such as `http://localhost:5173`. It is a literal string match, not a wildcard.
questions.asked: An obscure but real CORS bug; knowing who sends `null` is the tell of hands-on experience.

questions.q: In Node 24, this CORS check is meant to allow `example.com` and its subdomains. Which origin wrongly passes?
choices: `https://example.com.evil.io`, because the pattern matches anywhere in the host
`https://evilexample.com`, because nothing anchors the match to a dot or scheme
`http://app.example.com`, because the pattern ignores the scheme it arrived on
`https://EXAMPLE.com`, because regular expressions are case-insensitive by default
questions.why: `$` anchors only the end, so any host ending in `example.com`, including a registrable `evilexample.com`, matches. Parse the origin with `new URL()` and compare the scheme and hostname against an exact list or `host === 'example.com' || host.endsWith('.example.com')`. `example.com.evil.io` fails because of the anchor, and regexes are case-sensitive unless flagged `i`.
questions.asked: Regex allowlists are a common CORS bug; strong candidates parse the URL instead of pattern-matching strings.

questions.q: A React SPA signs users in with OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect. Which flow is the current recommendation?
choices: The implicit flow, which returns the access token directly in the URL fragment
The password grant, where the SPA posts the user's credentials to the provider
Authorization code with PKCE, ideally with a backend that keeps the tokens
Client credentials, with the client secret compiled into the SPA's JS bundle
questions.why: OAuth 2.1 and current best practice drop implicit and password grants; code + PKCE stops intercepted codes being redeemed, and a backend-for-frontend keeps tokens out of the browser behind an HttpOnly cookie. A secret shipped in a bundle is public, so client credentials is for servers only.
questions.asked: A standard modern-auth check; mentioning the BFF pattern marks a stronger answer.

questions.q: A teammate puts the user's email, phone number and home address into your API's JWT access token 'to save a database call'. What is the concern?
choices: Signed JWTs are only base64url-encoded, so anyone holding the token can read it
JWT signatures fail when the payload holds characters outside plain ASCII text
Tokens with more than five claims are rejected by most API gateways by default
The signature covers the header alone, so an attacker can edit the claims freely
questions.why: A JWS protects integrity, not confidentiality: the payload decodes in any browser, log or proxy that sees the token. Keep claims to identifiers and authorization data, and look up personal data server-side (or use an encrypted JWE if you truly must carry it). The signature covers both header and payload.
questions.asked: A basic misconception check; strong answers distinguish signing from encryption.

questions.q: An API issues JWT access tokens valid for 30 days and never checks a database. An employee is fired and their account disabled. What happens, and what is the usual design fix?
choices: The token stops working at once, since disabling the account changes the signing key
The token works until it expires; use short-lived access tokens and revocable refresh tokens
The token works for one more request only, since the API rechecks the account on refresh
The token stops working at the next deploy, since restarts clear the JWT validation cache
questions.why: Stateless tokens stay valid until `exp` because nothing is consulted, so 30 days is a 30-day revocation gap. Keep access tokens to minutes and put revocation on the refresh step, which checks the account; add a denylist only for urgent cases. Disabling an account does not rotate the signing key.
questions.asked: Revocation is the standard JWT trade-off question; strong candidates quantify the exposure window.

questions.q: A list endpoint lets clients sort with `?sort=`. The query values are parameterised, but the column is interpolated. What is the safe fix?
choices: Pass `sort` as `$2`, since placeholders work for column names as well as values
Escape single quotes in `sort` before interpolating it into the ORDER BY clause
Map `sort` through an allowlist of known column names and reject anything else
Wrap the query in a transaction so an injected statement is always rolled back
questions.why: Placeholders bind values, not identifiers, so `ORDER BY $2` sorts by a constant rather than a column. The input can still inject (`sort=(SELECT ...)` needs no quotes), so map allowed names such as `name`, `-price` to fixed SQL fragments. Rolling back does not stop data being read.
questions.asked: Sort and filter parameters are where injection survives in otherwise parameterised code.

questions.q: A Node API using MongoDB logs users in with this query, taking both fields straight from the JSON body. What can an attacker send?
choices: `{"password": "' OR '1'='1"}`, which Mongo turns into a query that is always true
`{"password": {"$ne": null}}`, which matches the user with any stored password
A 10 MB password string, which makes Mongo compare it slowly and time out
A password containing a null byte, which cuts off the comparison in Mongo
questions.why: JSON can carry objects, so an operator such as `$ne` or `$gt` replaces the literal comparison: NoSQL injection. Validate that both fields are strings (a schema with zod or similar), and never compare plaintext passwords anyway; look up by email and verify a hash. SQL quote tricks mean nothing to a Mongo query document.
questions.asked: Tests whether you know injection is not only a SQL problem; strong answers pair type validation with hashing.

questions.q: When validating API input, why is an allowlist (define what is valid) preferred over a denylist (block known-bad patterns)?
choices: Allowlists run faster, because regular expressions are compiled only once at startup
Denylists are prohibited by the OWASP ASVS for any API that handles personal data
Allowlists skip the need to encode output, since only safe input can reach storage
A denylist misses encodings and inputs nobody thought of; an allowlist rejects them
questions.why: Attackers only need one variant you did not list (case changes, Unicode, double encoding), whereas an allowlist of types, lengths, formats and enum values rejects everything unexpected by default. Validation still does not replace context-specific output encoding or parameterised queries.
questions.asked: A principle question; strong answers add that validation complements, not replaces, encoding and parameters.

questions.q: Should a JSON API reject request bodies that contain properties its schema does not define?
choices: Never; unknown fields are always ignored in JSON, as the RFC 8259 standard requires
It is a trade-off: strict rejection catches typos and mass assignment attempts early
Always; accepting unknown fields means your API is vulnerable to SQL injection
Only for GET requests, since query strings with unknown keys are always attacks
questions.why: Rejecting (zod `.strict()`, `JsonUnmappedMemberHandling.Disallow` in System.Text.Json) surfaces client mistakes and probing, while ignoring unknown fields is more tolerant of client versions. Either is defensible if you bind to a DTO; what is never fine is copying unknown fields into the entity. RFC 8259 says nothing about it.
questions.asked: Invites a nuanced answer; interviewers want the tolerant-reader versus strictness trade-off.

questions.q: A Node 24 search endpoint builds `new RegExp(req.query.q)` to filter names in memory. Beyond wrong results, what is the danger?
choices: A pattern like `^(a+)+$` with the right input can pin the event loop for seconds
RegExp objects built from user input are shared between requests and leak data
V8 compiles each new pattern to native code, which fills the disk over time
Patterns containing `/` characters close the literal and execute as JavaScript
questions.why: Nested quantifiers backtrack exponentially: `/^(a+)+$/` against 28 `a`s and a `!` takes over a minute in Node 24, and Node's single thread means every request waits. Escape user input into a literal match, or use plain `includes`, and cap input length. `new RegExp` never executes the pattern as code.
questions.asked: ReDoS is a Node-specific denial-of-service; strong candidates connect it to the single-threaded event loop.

questions.q: A Node API deep-merges `req.body` into a settings object with a naive recursive merge. An attacker sends `{"__proto__": {"isAdmin": true}}`. What happens?
choices: `JSON.parse` throws on the `__proto__` key, so the request fails with a 400
Only the settings object gains `isAdmin`, which the merge writes as an own property
`Object.prototype` gains `isAdmin`, so every plain object now reports it as true
Nothing, because Node 24 freezes `Object.prototype` by default for all modules
questions.why: `JSON.parse` creates an own `__proto__` key, and the merge then walks `target['__proto__']`, which is `Object.prototype`, and writes into it: prototype pollution. Skip `__proto__`, `constructor` and `prototype` keys, merge into `Object.create(null)`, or validate the body against a schema first. Node does not freeze prototypes unless you ask it to.
questions.asked: A JavaScript-specific API risk; strong candidates know why `JSON.parse` makes it reachable.

questions.q: An avatar upload endpoint accepts a file if its name ends in `.png` and the `Content-Type` header says `image/png`. What should it do instead?
choices: Also check the file size is under 10 MB, which is enough to rule out executables
Re-check the extension after lower-casing it, since `.PNG` bypasses the rule
Accept any file type, since scanning happens when the browser downloads it
Check the file's magic bytes, re-encode the image, and store it under a new name
questions.why: The name and `Content-Type` are chosen by the client, so both can lie. Inspect the content (magic bytes), ideally re-encode images with a library to strip payloads, store under a random server-chosen name outside the web root, and cap size. A size limit alone says nothing about what the file is.
questions.asked: Upload handling is a common take-home review point; interviewers want 'never trust the client's metadata'.

questions.q: Users can upload attachments, which the app serves back from `https://app.example.com/files/<id>` with the stored `Content-Type`. Why is that dangerous?
choices: An uploaded HTML or SVG file runs script on your origin, with the user's session
Browsers refuse to download files served from the same origin as the app itself
Serving files from the app origin prevents the CDN from caching any attachment
Stored content types expire after a day, so files are served as `text/plain`
questions.why: An SVG or HTML file rendered inline on your origin is stored XSS with full access to cookies and APIs. Serve user content from a separate sandbox domain, send `Content-Disposition: attachment` and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, and set the content type from your own allowlist.
questions.asked: Shows you think about uploads on the way out, not only on the way in.

questions.q: You notice a commit pushed to a public repo last week contains `.env` with the production database password. What is the first thing to do?
choices: Rewrite the Git history to remove the file, then force-push every branch
Make the repository private, so that nobody else can view the old commit
Rotate the password and any other secret in that file, then check the access logs
Add `.env` to `.gitignore` so the file cannot be committed again by accident
questions.why: Assume the secret is compromised: bots scrape public repos for credentials within minutes, and forks and clones keep the history. Rotating makes the leaked value useless; cleaning history and adding `.gitignore` are follow-ups, and secret scanning in CI prevents a repeat.
questions.asked: An incident-response instinct check; the only right first step is rotation.

questions.q: Your request-logging middleware writes every JSON body at `Information` level for debugging. Which endpoints make this a security problem?
choices: Only GET endpoints, whose query strings are already written by the web server
Login, signup and payment endpoints, whose bodies carry passwords and card data
Only admin endpoints, since their bodies may change other users' permissions
None, as long as the log files are stored on a disk that uses encryption at rest
questions.why: Logs are copied to aggregators, shared with support and kept for months, so passwords, tokens and card numbers there become a second, poorly guarded database (and a PCI problem). Redact sensitive fields by allowlist or skip bodies on sensitive routes. Disk encryption does not help once someone can read the logs.
questions.asked: A practical check; strong answers mention structured-logging redaction rather than 'be careful'.

questions.q: Why do JSON APIs send `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`?
choices: It stops browsers guessing a different type, such as running a JSON reply as script
It tells CDNs not to inspect the body, so that the response is never compressed
It disables CORS preflights for the response, since its type is fixed as JSON
It makes clients reject any response whose `Content-Length` header is missing
questions.why: MIME sniffing lets a browser treat a response as HTML or script if the content looks like it, which turns reflected input into XSS. `nosniff` makes the browser honour your `Content-Type` (and block mismatched script and style loads). It has no effect on compression, CORS or length headers.
questions.asked: A header most people set without knowing why; explaining the sniffing attack earns the credit.

questions.q: Two internal services call each other over the network. What does mutual TLS (mTLS) add over ordinary HTTPS?
choices: It encrypts the body twice, once for each service, so that proxies cannot read it
It replaces authorization, since any caller with a certificate may do anything
The client proves its identity with its own certificate, not only the server
It lets services skip certificate expiry checks, since both sides trust each other
questions.why: Normal TLS authenticates only the server; with mTLS the client presents a certificate too, so a service knows which workload is calling (service meshes automate this). You still authorise what that identity may do, and certificates still expire and rotate.
questions.asked: Service-to-service auth comes up once you mention microservices; separating identity from permission is key.

questions.q: Your public order URLs look like `/orders/10482`, with ids from an auto-increment column. Besides BOLA risk, what do sequential ids reveal?
choices: The database engine and its version, which attackers read from the id's width
The server's time zone, since ids are derived from the time of each insert
Nothing at all, provided that every order endpoint checks object ownership
Business volume: two orders a week apart show how many sales happened between
