questions.why: Sequential ids leak growth and volume to competitors and make enumeration trivial if an authorization check is ever missed. Keep the integer key internally and expose a random public id (UUIDv4 or v7, ULID). Ownership checks remain essential either way.
questions.asked: A design question with a business angle; good answers keep integer keys internal.

questions.q: An API listens on port 80 and replies `301` to `https://` for every request. Why is that not enough for API clients sending bearer tokens?
choices: API clients cannot follow a 301, so every request fails until the client is fixed
The first request, token included, already crossed the network unencrypted
A 301 changes POST to GET, which makes the redirected request lose its token
HTTPS redirects are cached for a year, so the certificate can never be rotated
questions.why: The redirect happens after the client has sent its headers in plain text, so the token is exposed on the first hop. For APIs, refuse plain HTTP outright (or do not listen on it) and use HSTS for browsers. Many clients do follow 301, which is exactly how the mistake stays hidden.
questions.asked: Distinguishes browser-oriented habits from API realities.

questions.q: An API returns validation errors as `{"detail": "'<script>…' is not a valid email"}`. When does echoing input become an XSS risk?
choices: Always, because JSON parsers run any script tags they find inside string values
Only when the API uses HTTP/1.1, since HTTP/2 escapes HTML in header frames
When the reply is served as HTML, or a client renders `detail` without escaping
Never, because problem details bodies are defined as plain text by RFC 9457
questions.why: Served as `application/problem+json` with `nosniff`, the browser will not render it, but a frontend that injects `detail` via `innerHTML` or `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` executes it. Prefer not echoing raw input, keep correct content types, and render messages as text. JSON parsing never runs script.
questions.asked: Tests whether you see the whole path from API response to rendered UI.

questions.q: Your API connects to Postgres with the `postgres` superuser because 'it's simpler'. Which change follows least privilege?
choices: Keep the superuser but rotate its password monthly and store it in a vault
Use a role with only the table rights the app needs, and another for migrations
Create one database role per end user, so every row is protected by the database
Keep the superuser but block the API's IP from connecting outside business hours
questions.why: If the app is compromised, via SQL injection for example, its database role is the blast radius; a role with only SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on its tables cannot drop schemas or read other databases. Migrations need DDL rights, so they run under a different role. Password rotation leaves the blast radius unchanged.
questions.asked: Least privilege is easy to state; interviewers want to hear the app and migration roles separated.

questions.q: Which automated test best guards against a BOLA regression on `GET /api/invoices/:id`?
choices: Log in as user B, request user A's invoice id, and assert a 404 response
Call the endpoint with no token at all, and assert a 401 response comes back
Request a random UUID that does not exist, and assert a 404 comes back
Log in as user A, request their own invoice, and assert a 200 response
questions.why: BOLA is 'authenticated but not the owner', so the test needs two real users and a real record owned by one of them. The anonymous test covers authentication, the random-id test covers not-found handling, and the owner test covers the happy path; none would catch a missing ownership filter.
questions.asked: Asks you to turn a security concept into a test; the two-user setup is the key detail.

questions.q: A security rule in your gateway blocks `DELETE` on `/api/users/*` for non-admins. The Express app uses `method-override` to honour `X-HTTP-Method-Override`. What is the gap?
choices: The gateway rewrites the header to GET, so admins cannot delete any user at all
`method-override` works only for form posts, so the header has no effect on JSON
Express 5 rejects the header by default, so the gateway rule is never reached
A non-admin POSTs with the header set to DELETE, and the app runs the delete
questions.why: The gateway sees a POST and lets it through; the app then treats it as DELETE. Enforce authorization in the application itself, and drop override headers unless you truly need them. `method-override` does honour a header you configure, and Express 5 does not strip it.
questions.asked: Tests whether you enforce rules where the decision is actually made, not only at the edge.

questions.q: A new Express app sends `X-Powered-By: Express` on every response. What is the honest assessment?
choices: It is a critical vulnerability, since attackers can take over any Express server
It is required by the HTTP spec, so removing it breaks some compliant clients
It is minor fingerprinting; turn it off with `app.disable('x-powered-by')`
It is harmless and in fact helps CDNs choose the right compression settings
questions.why: The header helps attackers pick exploits for your stack, but hiding it is defence in depth, not a fix; keeping dependencies patched matters far more. Disable it (or use Helmet), and similarly suppress Kestrel's `Server` header with `AddServerHeader = false`. No spec or CDN relies on it.
questions.asked: Checks for proportion; interviewers like candidates who rank findings by real risk.

questions.q: Your API decompresses gzip request bodies before JSON parsing and enforces a 1 MB limit on the compressed size. What attack does that leave open?
choices: A 1 MB gzip body can expand to gigabytes and exhaust the server's memory
Gzip bodies bypass TLS, so the compressed payload can be read on the wire
Compressed bodies skip JSON parsing, so schema validation never runs
Gzip headers carry file names, which attackers use for path traversal
questions.why: Compression ratios over 1000:1 are easy with repetitive data, so a small upload becomes a decompression bomb. Limit the decompressed size while streaming (Express's `express.json({ limit })` measures the inflated body), and consider refusing compressed requests on public endpoints. TLS and parsing are unaffected.
questions.asked: A deeper resource-exhaustion question; strong candidates say where to measure the limit.

questions.q: A cart API accepts `{ "productId": 7, "quantity": -3 }` and the order total goes negative, crediting the user. What was missing?
choices: An idempotency key, so that the negative line could not be submitted twice
A database transaction around the order insert and the payment capture
Business-rule validation: quantity must be a positive integer within a cap
HTTPS on the checkout route, so that the quantity could not be tampered with
questions.why: Type checks passed, since -3 is a number; the rule 'at least 1, at most N' was never enforced. Validate domain constraints at the API boundary (and ideally with a CHECK constraint in the database). The user edited their own request, so HTTPS and transactions do nothing.
questions.asked: Business-logic abuse is common in real bug bounties; interviewers want domain validation, not only types.

questions.q: A single-use coupon is checked with `SELECT used FROM coupons` and then marked with `UPDATE ... SET used = true`. A user fires 20 parallel checkout requests. What happens, and what fixes it?
choices: Only the first request runs, since Postgres serialises all queries on a table
Several requests read `used = false` first; use an atomic conditional update
All 20 fail, because Postgres throws deadlock errors on parallel UPDATE calls
Only the last request succeeds, since each UPDATE overwrites the one before it
questions.why: Check-then-act races: all requests can read the unused state before any update lands, so the coupon applies many times. Make the check and the change one statement, `UPDATE coupons SET used = true WHERE code = $1 AND used = false`, and proceed only if one row changed, or lock the row. Postgres runs these concurrently under default isolation.
questions.asked: Race-condition abuse is a favourite follow-up; the conditional update is the answer interviewers look for.

questions.q: `PATCH /api/me` lets a logged-in user change their email with no password check, and the reset flow emails the new address. Why is this a risk?
choices: Emails must be changed with PUT, since PATCH cannot touch unique columns
Changing an email invalidates every JWT, so the user is logged out at once
The new address must be confirmed by SMS, which the endpoint cannot send
A stolen session becomes a permanent takeover via the new email and reset
questions.why: Sensitive account changes (email, password, MFA) should require re-authentication, confirm the new address, and notify the old one, so a hijacked session cannot lock the owner out. The HTTP method is irrelevant, and changing email does not by itself revoke tokens.
questions.asked: Tests whether you think a step beyond the single request, to how an attacker chains flows.

questions.q: A WebSocket endpoint authenticates with the session cookie during the upgrade and does not check the `Origin` header. What attack is possible?
choices: Nothing, because browsers never send cookies on WebSocket upgrade requests
Cross-site WebSocket hijacking: any site opens the socket as the logged-in user
Slowloris: the socket is held open forever, until the server runs out of memory
Replay: an old WebSocket frame can be resent to repeat an earlier action
questions.why: WebSocket upgrades are not subject to CORS and do carry cookies (subject to SameSite), so a malicious page can connect and read messages as the victim. Check `Origin` against an allowlist during the upgrade, or authenticate with a short-lived ticket rather than a cookie.
questions.asked: Realtime features are common on CRUD apps; knowing that CORS does not cover WebSockets marks real experience.

questions.q: After login, your API redirects to `req.query.returnUrl`. What does an attacker do with `/login?returnUrl=https://evil.example/login`?
choices: Steal the session cookie, since the browser sends it to the redirect target
Bypass the login form, since the redirect runs before credentials are checked
Phish: your real login sends users to a fake page that asks them to sign in again
Inject SQL, since `returnUrl` is written straight into the session store
questions.why: An open redirect lends your domain's credibility to a phishing page and can leak OAuth codes or tokens in some flows. Accept only relative paths (starting with a single `/`) or an allowlist of hosts; ASP.NET Core's `Url.IsLocalUrl` helps. Cookies are not sent to a different domain.
questions.asked: Open redirects are low-effort findings; strong answers mention the OAuth angle.

questions.q: In ASP.NET Core 9, a teammate writes this CORS policy so that a React app on another origin can send cookies. What happens?
choices: It works, and every origin can now make credentialed calls and read the replies
Building the policy throws: a wildcard origin cannot be combined with credentials
It works, but the browser silently drops cookies because of `AllowAnyHeader()`
It compiles, but CORS headers are only sent after `UseAuthorization()` has run
questions.why: The CORS spec forbids `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` with credentials, and ASP.NET Core's policy builder throws an `InvalidOperationException` rather than emit an invalid policy. List the SPA's origins with `WithOrigins(...)`. `UseCors` belongs after `UseRouting` and before `UseAuthorization`, not after it.
questions.asked: Tests whether you know why the framework refuses this, which is the wildcard-with-credentials rule.

questions.q: A security review finds endpoints running in production that are missing from the team's OpenAPI document. Why does that matter?
choices: Undocumented endpoints return 404 to any client generated from the spec
OpenAPI tools reject the whole spec when real routes are missing from it
Browsers block calls to routes that are not declared in a published spec
Nobody reviews, tests or retires 'shadow' endpoints, so flaws linger there
questions.why: The spec is your inventory (OWASP API9): endpoints outside it escape security review, contract tests and deprecation plans, and are often old or debug routes. Generate the spec from code or diff routes against it in CI. Browsers and generators do not police real traffic against the spec.
questions.asked: Connects API documentation to security, a link many candidates miss.

questions.q: An operation in your OpenAPI spec declares `security: [{ bearerAuth: [] }]`. What does that do at runtime?
choices: Nothing by itself; it documents the requirement, and your code must still enforce it
It makes the web framework reject calls without a bearer token before the handler
It makes API gateways validate JWT signatures against the scheme's issuer
It stops the endpoint appearing in Swagger UI unless a token has been entered
questions.why: OpenAPI describes the API; enforcement comes from your middleware or `RequireAuthorization()`. Some gateways and validators can enforce parts of a spec, but only when you configure them to. A spec that says 'secured' over an unguarded route is a common audit finding.
questions.asked: A quick check that you separate documentation from enforcement.

questions.q: Your React app decides what to show by checking whether the error body's `detail` text contains 'already exists'. What should the API provide instead?
choices: A different HTTP status for each error, so the status alone identifies it
A stable machine-readable code, such as `type` or `code`, beside the message
An error message translated into every language the React app supports
An HTML fragment that the React app can insert directly into the page
questions.why: Human-readable text changes with wording tweaks and localisation, so clients need a stable identifier: RFC 9457's `type` URI or an extension like `code: "email_taken"`. There are far fewer status codes than error cases, and HTML fragments invite XSS.
questions.asked: Error contract design is a standard API design question; stable codes are the key point.

questions.q: A mobile app calls your API with a static API key compiled into the app. How should you treat that key?
choices: As secret, since app stores encrypt every binary they distribute to phones
As secret, if the key is obfuscated at build time with a string encoder
As public: anyone can extract it, so it identifies the app, not a user
As public, which is fine for writes but must never be used for reads
questions.why: Anything shipped to a device can be pulled out with a decompiler or proxy, so a baked-in key only identifies the client application for analytics or coarse limits. Real protection comes from per-user authentication (OAuth with PKCE) and server-side authorization. Obfuscation slows extraction, it does not prevent it.
questions.asked: Checks that you know client apps cannot keep secrets.

questions.q: Your API rate-limits per API key, and anyone can create unlimited free keys by signing up with any email address. What does that do to the limit?
choices: Nothing, since each key still has its own limit enforced on every request
It doubles the limit, because keys share a counter with their account owner
It makes the limiter return 503 instead of 429 once too many keys exist
It defeats it: an abuser spreads traffic over thousands of throwaway keys
questions.why: A per-key limit is only as strong as the cost of getting a key, so cheap identities (Sybil attacks) multiply the allowance. Verify sign-ups, cap keys per account, and add limits per account, payment method and IP range on top. Each key's own counter is honest; there are just too many of them.
questions.asked: Tests whether you think about how identities are issued, not only how they are counted.

questions.q: Some APIs require each request to be signed with an HMAC over the method, path, timestamp and body hash, instead of sending a bearer token. What does that add?
choices: It encrypts the body, so TLS can be turned off for signed requests
It removes the need for any secret, since the signature is its own key
A logged request cannot be edited or replayed, and the secret never travels
It lets the server skip authorization, since signed callers are trusted
questions.why: With request signing (as in AWS SigV4), the secret stays on the client and each signature covers one specific request and time, so a captured request cannot be altered or reused later. A bearer token that leaks in a log can be replayed until it expires. Signing gives integrity, not confidentiality, and authorization still applies.
questions.asked: A deeper comparison of credential styles; strong answers mention replay windows and clock skew.

questions.q: Your API logs the client-supplied `X-Request-Id` header as-is into plain-text logs. What can a malicious client do?
choices: Inject newlines to forge log lines, or send a huge value to bloat storage
Overwrite other users' log entries by reusing their request id values
Run shell commands on the log server by putting backticks in the header
Nothing, because logging libraries drop headers that were set by clients
questions.why: Untrusted text with CR/LF can fake entries such as 'admin login succeeded' and mislead investigations; very long values cost money. Validate the id's format and length (or generate your own and echo it), and use structured JSON logging that escapes values. Logs are appended, not overwritten.
questions.asked: Log injection is a subtle input-handling issue; good answers mention structured logging.

questions.q: A cursor-paginated API encodes the cursor as base64 of `{"lastId": 120, "ownerId": 7}` and trusts `ownerId` from it on the next page. What is the flaw?
choices: Base64 adds a third to the cursor's size, which may exceed URL length limits
The cursor expires when the server restarts, which breaks deep pagination
The ids should be encoded as strings, since JSON integers overflow in base64
Clients can decode it, set another `ownerId`, and page through someone's data
questions.why: Base64 is encoding, not protection; an 'opaque' cursor is still client input. Take the owner from the authenticated user on every page, and sign or encrypt cursors (HMAC) if tampering with their contents would matter. The size and number-format concerns are not security issues.
questions.asked: Tests whether you treat every value that round-trips through the client as untrusted.

questions.q: Your GraphQL `User.email` field checks that the viewer is the user or an admin, but only in the top-level `user(id:)` resolver. What is the gap?
choices: `post { author { email } }` reaches the field through another path unchecked
The check runs after the query completes, so the data was already returned
GraphQL resolvers cannot read the viewer, so the check never actually runs
Admins are blocked too, since GraphQL checks each field for every role
questions.why: A GraphQL graph has many paths to the same type, so authorization belongs on the field or type (or in the business layer it calls), not on one entry point. Resolvers receive the request context, including the viewer, so field-level checks are straightforward.
questions.asked: Field-level authorization is the GraphQL-specific BOLA; interviewers look for 'authorise in the business layer'.

questions.q: How does a gRPC client normally send a bearer access token with each call?
choices: Inside every Protobuf request message, as a field named `token` or `auth`
As call metadata under the `authorization` key, sent as an HTTP/2 header
As a cookie, since gRPC channels share the browser's cookie jar by default
In the TLS client certificate, which gRPC requires for every single call
questions.why: gRPC metadata maps to HTTP/2 headers, so `authorization: Bearer ...` works with standard middleware (ASP.NET Core authentication applies to gRPC services too), and call credentials can attach it automatically. Putting tokens in messages mixes auth into every contract; client certificates are an option, not a requirement.
questions.asked: A quick gRPC check that shows you know it is still HTTP underneath.

questions.q: Swagger UI for your API is publicly reachable in production. What is the balanced assessment?
choices: It is always a critical flaw, since 'Try it out' bypasses the API's authentication
It is harmless, since attackers cannot call an endpoint they found in the docs
It is required, since OpenAPI clients download the UI to generate their code
It maps your attack surface; fine for public APIs, restrict it for internal ones
questions.why: The UI sends ordinary requests, so auth still applies, but it hands out every route and schema, internal ones included. Public APIs publish docs deliberately; internal or admin APIs should hide them or put them behind auth. Clients download the JSON spec, not the UI.
questions.asked: Checks that you can weigh a finding instead of labelling everything critical.

questions.q: An ASP.NET Core app maps `/health` with a response writer that dumps every check's details, including connection strings and exception messages, with no auth. What should change?
choices: Nothing, as health endpoints must be public so the load balancer can reach them
Rename the route to something unguessable, keeping the full details available
Serve a bare status publicly and put detailed output behind auth or a private port
Remove health checks entirely, since orchestrators can detect crashes on their own
questions.why: Load balancers only need 'Healthy' or a 503; details such as hosts, versions and error text help attackers. Split liveness/readiness from a detailed diagnostics endpoint that needs auth or is bound to an internal interface. Renaming is obscurity, and removing health checks breaks graceful deployment.
questions.asked: A real misconfiguration pattern; strong answers separate what orchestrators need from what operators need.

questions.q: In Node 24, your server calls a partner API with `fetch(url, { headers: { Authorization: 'Bearer ...' } })`, and the partner replies 302 to a different origin. What does `fetch` do with the header?
choices: It forwards the header to the new origin, since redirects keep every request header
It refuses to follow the redirect, since a cross-origin 302 is a network error
It follows the redirect and drops `Authorization`, since the origin has changed
It follows the redirect and converts the bearer token into a cookie header instead
questions.why: The Fetch standard, implemented by Node's undici, strips `Authorization` on a cross-origin redirect so credentials are not leaked to another host. If the new host genuinely needs a token, handle the redirect yourself with `redirect: 'manual'` and decide explicitly. Older HTTP clients did forward it, which caused real leaks.
questions.asked: A detail that matters when you integrate with third parties; shows you know client behaviour, not only server behaviour.

questions.q: An API gateway validates JWTs and forwards requests to internal services with an `X-User-Id` header, which the services trust. What must also be true for this to be safe?
choices: The header must be base64-encoded, so that clients cannot guess what it holds
The services must be unreachable except via the gateway, which strips client copies
The services must re-issue the JWT, so that each hop carries a fresh signature
The gateway must use HTTP/2, since HTTP/1.1 lets clients add duplicate headers
questions.why: If a client can reach a service directly, or send its own `X-User-Id` that the gateway passes through, it can be anyone. Strip incoming copies at the gateway, lock the network so only the gateway can call services, or forward the signed token and let each service verify it. Encoding does nothing.
questions.asked: Trust boundaries between gateway and services are a common system-design probe.

questions.q: Why do many teams load production secrets from a secrets manager (Azure Key Vault, AWS Secrets Manager) rather than plain environment variables baked into the deployment?
choices: Environment variables are world-readable by any user on a Linux server
Environment variables cannot hold values longer than 256 characters
Secrets managers are faster to read, which shortens the app's startup time
A vault gives access control, audit logs and rotation without redeploying
questions.why: Env vars are fine at runtime but usually live in pipeline settings or files with broad access, and they leak into crash dumps, child processes and debug pages. A manager centralises who can read what, records access and lets you rotate. Env vars are readable by the process owner and root, not every user.
questions.asked: A practical ops question; strong answers mention managed identity so the app needs no bootstrap secret.

questions.q: What security benefit does committing `package-lock.json` give a Node API?
choices: npm scans every locked package for malware each time it runs an install
It pins exact versions and hashes, so builds cannot pull in a changed package
It stops `npm audit` warnings for packages that are listed in the lockfile
It prevents transitive dependencies being installed without your approval
questions.why: The lockfile records exact versions and integrity hashes, so `npm ci` installs the reviewed tree and fails if a tarball changes; a new malicious patch release is not picked up silently. Updates then arrive as reviewable diffs. It does not scan for malware or silence audits.
questions.asked: Supply-chain awareness is increasingly expected; mentioning `npm ci` in CI is the practical detail.

questions.q: Which TLS configuration is appropriate for a public API in 2026?
choices: TLS 1.0 and later, so that every older client is still able to connect
SSL 3.0 and later, since it is the most widely supported protocol version
TLS 1.3 only, removing TLS 1.2 because it is now considered insecure
TLS 1.2 and 1.3, with TLS 1.0 and 1.1 disabled as deprecated protocols
questions.why: TLS 1.0 and 1.1 were formally deprecated (RFC 8996) and SSL 3.0 is broken. TLS 1.2 with modern cipher suites remains secure and widely needed, while 1.3 is preferred. 1.3-only is reasonable for some internal services but can lock out older clients.
questions.asked: A baseline hygiene check; knowing 1.2 is still acceptable avoids over-correcting.

questions.q: A JSON-only API adds `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'`. Why bother, when it serves no HTML?
choices: If a response is ever rendered as a page, nothing loads and it cannot be framed
CSP makes the browser validate the response body against the JSON schema
Without CSP, browsers refuse to send cookies on requests to the API origin
CSP compresses JSON responses, since it tells the browser no scripts will run
questions.why: Browsers may render an API response opened directly or misdetected; a deny-all policy means injected markup cannot load scripts or be embedded for clickjacking. It is cheap defence in depth, alongside `nosniff` and correct content types. CSP has nothing to do with cookies, schemas or compression.
questions.asked: Shows you understand security headers by their effect, not as a copy-pasted list.

questions.q: A webhook provider lets you roll the signing secret. How should your receiver behave during the change-over?
choices: Stop verifying signatures during the rotation window so that no event is lost
Accept a signature made with either the old or the new secret, then drop the old
Reject all events until the new secret is live on every instance of the app
Ask the provider to send each event twice, once per secret, and dedupe them
questions.why: Deploying a new secret is not instant across instances, and the provider may sign in-flight retries with the old one, so accept both for a short overlap, then remove the old. Providers such as Stripe send multiple signatures during a roll for this reason. Pausing verification opens a window for forged events.
questions.asked: Operational detail that reveals whether you have run webhooks in production.

questions.q: Your API verifies JWTs by fetching keys from the URL in the token's `jku` header. Why is that dangerous?
choices: Fetching keys over HTTPS on every request always exceeds the API's timeout budget
An attacker points `jku` at their own key set, signs a token, and it verifies
`jku` is only defined for encrypted JWEs, so signed tokens fail to validate
The `jku` URL is logged on every request, which leaks the identity provider
questions.why: Any header in the token is attacker-controlled, so letting it choose where keys come from lets anyone mint valid tokens. Configure the JWKS URL for your issuer yourself, cache it, and use `kid` only to pick among those trusted keys. The same principle applies to `alg`: pin it.
questions.asked: A deep JWT question; the principle 'the token must not choose its own trust anchor' is what interviewers want.

questions.q: A multi-tenant SaaS API takes the tenant from an `X-Tenant-Id` header on each request. What must the API check?
choices: That the header value is a valid UUID, since a well-formed id cannot be forged
That the header matches the subdomain, since browsers cannot change the Host
Nothing, as long as the header is sent only by the company's own frontend
That the authenticated user belongs to that tenant before any data is touched
questions.why: The header is client input, so switching it is BOLA across tenants unless membership is verified (or the tenant is derived from the token or session). Then scope every query by that tenant. A well-formed id can still be someone else's, and any client can call the API directly.
questions.asked: Multi-tenancy is common in B2B CRUD jobs; interviewers look for 'verify membership, then scope every query'.

questions.q: A multi-tenant API on Postgres adds row-level security policies using `current_setting('app.tenant_id')`, set per request. What does this buy you?
choices: It replaces application authorization, so handlers no longer need tenant checks
It speeds up every query, since Postgres skips rows for other tenants on disk
A forgotten `WHERE tenant_id` returns no foreign rows, since Postgres filters them
It encrypts each tenant's rows with a different key, so dumps are unreadable
questions.why: RLS is defence in depth: the database applies the policy to every query, so a missed filter leaks nothing. Beware that table owners and superusers bypass RLS unless it is forced, and that the setting must be reset per connection, which matters with pooling. It is not encryption and does not replace role checks.
questions.asked: An advanced multi-tenancy answer; mentioning the owner-bypass and pooling caveats shows depth.

questions.q: Which `Cache-Control` value should an OAuth token endpoint or login response that returns tokens carry?
choices: `private, max-age=3600`, so the browser reuses the token until it expires
`public, max-age=60`, so a CDN absorbs repeated logins for a short time
`no-cache`, so the response is stored but revalidated before any reuse
`no-store`, so no browser or intermediary cache keeps a copy of the tokens
questions.why: OAuth 2.0 requires `no-store` on token responses: credentials must not sit in any cache, shared or private. `no-cache` still allows storage with revalidation, and anything `public` risks serving one user's token to another.
questions.asked: Links caching knowledge to security; the no-cache versus no-store distinction is the tell.

questions.q: What should a security audit log entry for 'user role changed' contain?
choices: Who acted, on which user, old and new role, when, source IP and the outcome
The full request and response bodies, including tokens, for complete replay
Only the target user's id, since the rest can be rebuilt from the database
The acting user's password hash, so that later disputes can be verified
questions.why: Audit logs answer 'who did what to whom, when, from where, and did it work', so they need actor, target, change, time, origin and result, kept tamper-resistant and retained. Tokens and password hashes must never be logged, and the database shows only the current state, not the history.
questions.asked: Tests whether you log for investigations, not just debugging.
